In everyday informal English, a guy is simply a man or a boy. It's casual and friendly — not rude, not formal.

  • "He's a nice guy." → He's a pleasant man.
  • "Some guy called for you." → A man called for you.
  • "Who is that guy?" → Who is that man?

You use it when talking casually about a male person. You would not use it in formal writing (like a job application or a business letter) — it's too informal for those settings.
"Guys" in the plural — the most important thing to learn

When you say guys (plural), something interesting happens: the word becomes gender-neutral. It no longer means only men. It refers to any group of people — all men, all women, or a mix.

  • "Hey guys, dinner is ready!" — said to a group of women.
  • "You guys coming tonight?" — said to a mixed group.
  • "My guys handled everything." — My people / my team handled everything.

This is one of the most commonly used words in American English. Think of "guys" as an informal way of saying "everyone" or "you all" when addressing a group. It's the American English equivalent of "y'all" in Southern American English.

An important nuance: Because the word originally referred only to men, some people — particularly women — may not like being addressed as "guys." It's not offensive to most people, but if you want to be more inclusive, you can use "folks," "everyone," or "you all" instead. In professional settings, "everyone" or "team" is often preferred.

Occasionally, in very informal speech, yes — but this is much less common than the plural use.

  • "She's a good guy." — This happens in casual conversation, meaning she's a good person.
  • "She's a tough guy." — She's a tough, resilient person.

This singular gender-flexible use is growing but is not yet standard. Most speakers still use "guy" in the singular to mean a male person. In the plural ("guys"), gender-neutrality is fully accepted and very common.

This meaning is completely separate from the people-meaning. A guy (also called a guy wire or guy rope) is a rope, wire, or cable that is used to hold something in place or keep it from falling or swaying.

You've likely seen these without knowing the word: the diagonal cables holding up telephone poles, radio towers, tall cranes, or tent poles are all "guys."

  • "Tighten the guys before the storm arrives."
  • "The mast is supported by steel guys."

You'll encounter this meaning in contexts like camping, construction, sailing, and engineering. It has nothing to do with people.
British English: a Guy Fawkes effigy

In British English, a guy (often written as "Guy") refers to a dummy — a human-shaped figure made of old clothes stuffed with newspaper or straw — made to look like Guy Fawkes. Guy Fawkes was a real historical person who famously tried to blow up the British Parliament on November 5, 1605.

Every year in the UK, on Bonfire Night (November 5th), people burn these effigies on large bonfires as part of a national tradition. Children historically made these dummies and carried them through the streets, asking passersby: "A penny for the Guy!" — meaning, give me a coin so I can celebrate the holiday.

Unless you're in the UK around November, you're unlikely to hear this meaning in everyday conversation. But it's useful to know if you read British literature or watch British TV.
Old British meaning: a strangely dressed person (now rare)

Because Guy Fawkes effigies were often dressed in wild, ridiculous clothing, the word "guy" was once used in British English to describe someone who looked odd, absurd, or was dressed in a ridiculous way.

  • "What a guy he looks!" — What a strange-looking person!

This usage is now very old-fashioned and almost never heard in modern speech. You might come across it in 19th-century British novels, but not in everyday conversation today.
All meanings, in order of how commonly you'll encounter them

1. A man or boy — the most common, everyday meaning.
"He's a funny guy."

2. "Guys" = any group of people — extremely common; gender-neutral in plural.
"Hey guys, let's go!"

3. Any person, regardless of gender (singular) — informal, less common, growing in use.
"She's a great guy to work with."

4. A rope or wire used to steady something — technical meaning, unrelated to people.
"The tent needs more guys in the wind."

5. A Guy Fawkes effigy — British cultural meaning, specific to November 5th.
"The children made a guy for Bonfire Night."

6. A strangely dressed or odd-looking person — British, now rare and old-fashioned.
"What a guy she looks in that costume!"
The one thing to always remember

If you learn nothing else, learn this: "guys" (plural) in casual, everyday English — especially American English — means any group of people. It's one of the most commonly used informal words in the English language. You will hear it constantly in conversations, TV shows, movies, and daily life.
